draft.title: Abstract nouns that summarise
card: An abstract noun names an idea, not a physical thing. Examples are decision, failure, injustice and change.
A writer can use one to sum up a whole idea from the sentence before. Example: The council closed the pool without asking residents. This decision angered many families.
In that example, this decision stands for the whole act of closing the pool. The writer does not need to repeat it.
The noun also adds a view. Calling the closure an injustice judges it, while calling it a decision only names it. The new sentence can then build on the idea.
draft.remember: An abstract noun packs an earlier idea into one phrase and can add the writer's view.

a.q: Which underlined phrase sums up the idea of the first sentence? Sentence: The school banned phones from every classroom. ___ made some students frustrated.
opts: This ban
The students
Every classroom
The school's phones
a.why: This ban is an abstract noun that sums up the whole action of banning phones. The students, classrooms and phones are things or people named in the sentence, and none of them sums up the action.
a.clue: Which phrase names the whole action, not a person or place?

b.q: Ravi writes: The factory dumped waste into the creek for years. This negligence killed the fish. What does this negligence do in the second sentence?
opts: Sums up the dumping and judges it as careless
Names the creek that the fish lived in
Repeats the first sentence in the same words
Describes the fish before they died
b.why: This negligence points back to the whole act of dumping waste and adds a judgement that it was careless. It does not repeat the sentence word for word, because it packs the idea into a new phrase.
b.clue: Look at what the noun refers back to and what opinion it adds.

b.best: Sums up the dumping and judges it as careless
